A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InFOM work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original ExORL and OGBench evaluations, method comparisons and hyperparameter ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds intention visualizations, RT-1/SimplerEnv evaluation and further controlled analyses.

M1.justification: V2 changes the SARSA bootstrap target's conditioning from (s,a) to (s′,a′) and reverses the expectile residual from Q−Qhat to Qz−Q, with corresponding pseudocode changes (Sections 4.3–4.4; Algorithms 1–2). Appendix F.1 also adapts InFOM to frozen β-VAE image embeddings. These are bounded revisions to the documented procedure; the PDFs do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The original 36 state-based and four image-based benchmark tasks are retained. Appendix F.1 adds training on real robot data from RT-1 and evaluation on SimplerEnv's google_robot_pick_coke_can task, substantially extending coverage beyond the original simulated datasets.

E2.justification: The eight main baselines and existing FB/HILP intention-encoder comparisons are retained. The new robotics comparison evaluates standalone behavioral cloning alongside ReBRAC and DINO+ReBRAC; standalone BC was not a reported comparator in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds protocols using the entire RT-1 dataset for both training stages, frozen image embeddings, dense-reward ReBRAC controls, and pre-training/fine-tuning dataset-size sweeps. It extends the future-state sampling sweep to N=1 and additional tasks. Existing benchmark training budgets remain unchanged, while jaco's previously stated dense rewards are redescribed as sparse without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds intention-clustering case studies, dense-versus-sparse reward controls, removal of BC regularization, and dataset-size sensitivity studies (Figures 4, 6, 10–13). The existing future-state-count ablation is expanded to eight tasks in Figure 14. Original encoder comparisons, convergence analyses and other hyperparameter ablations are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across eight seeds for state-based tasks and four for image-based tasks. V2 extends this existing practice to additional experiments without changing uncertainty estimation or documenting increased repetitions of retained experiments.

E6.justification: All 344 mean-and-standard-deviation entries in Table 4 are identical. V2 nevertheless adds substantial results: a reported 34% advantage over DINO+ReBRAC in the new robotics comparison, improved ReBRAC performance with dense jaco rewards, dataset-size trends, BC-removal outcomes and intention-clustering findings. These are additional results rather than improved scores on the original benchmark comparison.

T1.justification: Reversing the residual under the unchanged asymmetric-loss definition corrects its mathematical consistency with the claimed upper-expectile maximization. Target-field conditioning is also corrected in the flow equations. The consistency assumption, ELBO/information-bottleneck derivation and asymptotic GPI argument otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: intention-conditioned flow occupancy learning and implicit GPI for offline pre-training and adaptation. The reported 1.8× return and 36% success-rate improvements on the original benchmark suite remain unchanged; added experiments primarily support existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations involving reward sparsity, BC protection against out-of-distribution actions and overestimated values, data requirements, and Monte Carlo estimation variability. It interprets t-SNE clusters as intention alignment and newly discusses poor end-to-end pixel learning on RT-1. The original limitation concerning intention inference from adjacent transitions is retained.

D1.justification: New disclosures include fourfold scaling of jaco returns for aggregation, RT-1's 73,499 episodes and reuse across training stages, and frozen β-VAE versus DINO representations. The reproducibility statement largely relocates existing JAX, A6000 hardware, runtime and code-access information from v1's appendix.

R1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly distinguishes the setting from meta-RL and multi-task RL through task-description and reward-supervision requirements. Related citations are added, alongside references for RT-1, SimplerEnv, t-SNE and latent-space generative modeling. Positioning relative to TD flows and successor-representation methods remains stable.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: background formulations and algorithms move to appendices, Section 5.2 foregrounds intention visualizations, and the original encoder and convergence studies move to Appendices F.2–F.3. The supplement is reorganized around problem-setting discussions, visualizations and additional experiments, with document-wide citation and terminology edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds trajectory/t-SNE panels, a robotics comparison and several controlled-analysis plots. The original sampling-count bars become an expanded line plot in Figure 14, while other hyperparameter panels are rearranged in Figure 15. Existing figures and algorithm displays are relocated, alongside substantial typography and layout changes.

improvement.justification: V2 adds controlled tests of reward sparsity, regularization removal and data requirements that v1 lacked, alongside intention visualizations and expanded sampling analysis. These substantially strengthen evidence for the design choices, while corrected bootstrap conditioning and expectile direction improve mathematical clarity. The robotics extension remains limited to one simulated task with fixed embeddings and an inconsistent return/success-rate label, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.
